text: One Ukrainian FPV pilot's ground station was destroyed by artillery in July 2023.
Ukrainian quadcopter crews usually had two or more operators: one flying and one spotting, matching the feed to a map.
The Ukrainian volunteer drone unit on the southern front in March 2023 had 15 people.
R18 crews were a pilot, a navigator and a sapper, trained in groups of three or four crews.
RUSI's later design rule is for each platoon to be able to generate two UAVs so that launches can be staggered; this is a recommendation, not a 2023 establishment.

observations.subject: UAVs each platoon should be able to generate

notes: No 2023 source found gives a brigade's or battalion's drone holdings for the 72nd or the 47th.

text: Ukraine had 3,000–5,000 FPVs in 2022.
In mid-2023 the head of a Ukrainian aerial-reconnaissance centre estimated Ukraine made fewer than 10,000 quality FPVs a month, against 45,000–50,000 for Russia.

claimants.name: head of a Ukrainian aerial-reconnaissance centre

text: Ukrainian defence-ministry figures imply about 1.2 million FPVs received in 2024 and 3 million in 2025.
RUSI found 60–80% of Ukrainian FPVs failing to reach their targets in 2024.
CSIS reports FPV success of 10–15% under jamming, rising to a claimed 70–80% with terminal autonomy.
Russian fibre-optic FPVs arrived in August 2024.
Ukraine had about 1 in 10 FPV teams on fibre-optic control by May 2025.
Ukrainian fibre-optic FPV reach grew to more than 40 km by July 2025.
By 2026 the Vampire had become a mass reusable bomber costing about $8,500, made at about 100,000 a year and flying about a dozen sorties per airframe.
The Unmanned Systems Forces became a separate branch of the Ukrainian armed forces in June 2024.
The Drone Line, announced in February 2025, aimed at a kill zone 10–15 km deep.
By 2024 RUSI found the battlefield dense with observation within 3 km of the line and taskable to 40 km.
Russia's Rubikon centre made Ukrainian drone teams a priority target, with over 25% of its strikes on them by September 2025.

text: Delta's Mission Control was handling about 106,000 drone missions a month in 2024.

effect: link range cut from 8–15 km to about 500 m; quadcopters lost or crashed
rationale: CNAS: under Bakhmut jamming a Mavic 3 lost control after about 500 m; near Huliaipole one unit lost three Mavics in two weeks and a jammed Matrice crashed.

effect: bomber drones could not get in; usually not committed
rationale: RUSI: with Russian EW active the night bombers "could not get in and usually were not committed".

effect: FPVs unusable for large parts of the day
rationale: RUSI was told that for large parts of the day EW means FPVs "simply cannot be used"; one 47th Brigade flight ended in signal loss, possibly jammed.

counter: Russian EW adaptation to new Ukrainian drone links
measure: new Ukrainian drone control or navigation system
effect: jammed across the front within 6–12 weeks (lag 42–84 days; lower bound given)
rationale: RUSI: a new system was at peak for about two weeks, degraded over four more and was jammed across the front within 6–12 weeks.

counter: flying only in EW gaps and frequent frequency changes
effect: drones kept flying as spotters through summer 2023
rationale: CNAS: Ukrainian spotter drones flew "only … when they found EW gaps" and changed frequencies often.

effect: operators located and targeted within 5–6 minutes
rationale: AeroScope reads DJI broadcast IDs and locates pilots; Russian users targeted and killed Ukrainian operators, finding them in as little as five or six minutes.

effect: drone and pilot no longer broadcast to AeroScope
rationale: Open-source software from May 2022 let pilots switch off DJI Remote ID; Ukraine eventually had software to disable the tracking.

effect: blocked the Remote ID switch-off, about a month after it appeared
rationale: DJI drones from about June 2022 had firmware that blocked switching off Remote ID.

effect: takes control of drones; geolocates operators
rationale: Shipovnik-Aero can take control of drones and geolocate their operators.

effect: forced landing and capture of commercial drones; pilots exposed
rationale: Russian EW forced Ukrainian commercial drones to land and turned them against their owners; DJI take-off position exposes pilots.
Russian EW could intercept and decrypt Ukrainian Motorola traffic in near real time in 2023.

effect: infantry shelter from small drone-dropped grenades
rationale: At Vuhledar Russian marines waited, "step aside behind a tree", and kept fighting.

effect: smoke did not save the Russian column
rationale: On 6 February 2023 Ukrainian artillery fired into the head of a Russian smoke screen behind which vehicles had bunched up.
RUSI: smoke blinds the view from UAVs that command posts use, so Ukrainian units fired smoke on only 3% of missions.

measure: RF jamming of drone control links
effect: success under jamming from 10–15% to a claimed 70–80%
rationale: CSIS: FPV success of 10–15% under jamming rises to a claimed 70–80% with terminal autonomy.

measure: RF jamming of drone control links
effect: harder to jam than digital video
rationale: Analog FPV video is harder to jam than digital, but unencrypted.

effect: over 25% of Rubikon strikes on drone teams
rationale: Rubikon made Ukrainian drone teams a priority target, with over 25% of its strikes on them by September 2025.
